text: Course 7 had you build structured logging into an integration from the start — gs.error and gs.info calls at defined checkpoints, backed by a retry and backoff strategy. That trail exists for exactly this moment: a production integration failing, and someone needing to find out why.

A failed integration investigation starts with that checkpoint log, but it rarely ends there. Pull the log entries for the failing transaction first — which checkpoint it died at, how many retries ran, what each attempt returned. Then widen the lens with tools from earlier in this course.

The Slow Request Log tells you whether this integration's calls are running slow compared to their own baseline — useful when the symptom is timing out rather than erroring outright. The Script Performance Profiler tells you whether the delay is in your own transform code, or whether the instance handed off quickly and the delay is happening somewhere external. Read together with the checkpoint log, these usually answer the first real question before you touch a line of code.

That first question is the fork that actually matters: is this a genuine bug in the integration's own logic, or is the cause sitting entirely outside your instance? A bug fails on the same record shape every time, and the Profiler shows the time sink inside your own script. An external cause looks different — and it has three common signatures. An outage: the external system is simply down, no response or a five-hundred-series error, nothing to deploy. A 429: the external system is actively telling you to slow down. An expired OAuth token: the call fails authentication, typically a 401, even though the request itself was built correctly.

Each of those three external signatures needs a different fix, and none of them is a code fix. An outage means waiting it out while retry and backoff absorb the gap, and communicating status. A 429 means adjusting call volume or timing. An expired token means refreshing or reconfiguring the credential, not debugging the payload.

Diving into the script editor under pressure feels productive, but it's exactly backward when the real cause is external — no code change un-rate-limits an API or brings a vendor system back online. Checking the status codes first is what separates a fast diagnosis from a wasted hour. Next: a flow that looks stuck — and the real distinction between one that's genuinely failed and one that's just waiting on an approval.
